utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sorry we have a delayed start because the previous trial ran overtime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As I promised, I believe I will complete the redirect examination today within 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, yesterday I was unable to understand the answer you gave to Ms. Gopalan about whether or not you knew personally the lawyer Destan Rukiqi. Did you know him as a lawyer at all?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did he work in Pristina or in another town?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me about Mr. Rukiqi. Was he a well known attorney in Pristina in the territory of the district court of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't really well known or reputed or actually professional enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Rukiqi a known advocate of human rights as is stated in some texts? Did you have personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I heard of that for the first time yesterday. He didn't engage in such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The cross-examination about the topic I'm going to deal with now lasted almost an entire session. Now you said that for [indiscernible] personal injuries the subject matter jurisdiction is with the municipal court and the municipal public prosecutor. So tell me, was ever an investigation against you launched before the municipal court in Pristina? So I will not focus only on the offence of committing crimes on the part of a judge. So was any investigation launched against you, were any proceedings launched against you in connection with your work, that is, did Albanians appear before court to testify against you? So were there criminal proceedings pending against you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never. Nor were there any objections to my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As for the objection to the work of a judge, to who can such an objection be uttered?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the president of the court. That's what the law provides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The case involving the illegal MUP, was any objection filed against you in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question refers to something Ms. Gopalan asked you toward the end of the cross-examination. It has to do with a number of matters that followed after the question was asked whether the court in Pristina worked professionally and whether it upheld the law, et cetera. But you didn't provide a direct answer to one of Ms. Gopalan's questions, and I believe we should hear that answer. I will immediately provide a reference. Page 13088 of yesterday's transcript. It's toward the top of the page. I think it even starts in line 1. You were asked, do you cover the work of the MUP, that is, the alleged torture of the suspects held in detention, but you didn't provide a clear answer. So did you -- was the work of the police within the scope of your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't. I wasn't authorised to do so, nor is it part of my job description. I have no direct connections with the work of the police. It's the prosecutor who co-operates with them, so I couldn't have done that at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will take this a bit further. In which part of the investigation do you have direct contact with the police and how, in which cases?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Law on Criminal Procedure, I as an investigating judge can issue an order to the -- to the police to conduct a certain investigative measure, that is, search a home or issue a certificate about evidence taken. Likewise, the police -- I can also order the police to secure the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Stop. What does that mean, secure the site?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The site must be secured so that nobody can manipulate the evidence so the site is fenced off and nobody is allowed access to that location where there may be traces or some objects used in the commitment of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This will be important for us later. Please continue. What else could the police do?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, the police authorised by the investigating judge could carry out investigative measures, one of which is if the indictee fails to respond to a summons, the investigating judge can issue an order which must be executed by the police and bring in the person to be interviewed by the investigating judge. This applies to witnesses also.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from what you have mentioned in the framework of an investigation, that is investigative measures, can the police ask questions or have demands toward the investigating judge or even issue orders?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The following question is the entire verdict for the parallel MUP case is included in the case file. Does this include the reasoning of the verdict?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a reasoning that is over 130 pages long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask our assistant Ms. O'Leary to prepare the video-clips, and I would like to see the portion from 17 minutes, 18 seconds, and then some 6 or 7 seconds of that clip. After that I'll have a specific question. Is everything all right for the witness also, Mr. Usher? Let's start.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should have started earlier. Yes, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person in the video-clip? Can you see the person now passing and the other who continues moving in front of him?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did KVM or the OSCE ever have uniformed people in their escort like these two men?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Ms. O'Leary, can we try to go back in that video-clip and take a look at the patch on the sleeve of that man's jacket. Stop it here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen such a patch?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several times. That's the KLA insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is connected with your conversation that you had with General Drewienkiewicz on the 17th of January. I believe that you spoke in the police station in Stimlje. Did General Drewienkiewicz mention the presence of KLA forces at the site in the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the next clip from 17 minutes, 30 something seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this. Thank you, this will do. You saw what was done here, did anybody have the right when we speak about securing the site, to arrive there before the investigative services of the country arrived there? This was before the NATO bombing, you saw what this person was doing.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody had such authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And I must go back to the conversation with General Drewienkiewicz again. Did the KVM try to secure the site in Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drewienkiewicz did not mention that, but they are not authorised to do so either, but he had no suggestion to that effect, nor did we speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This again has to do with the bodies that were autopsied. We speak about the -- their number being 40. Do you know, did the OTP or anybody else even in previous trials such as Milutinovic or Milosevic, did anybody speak about another number of the persons killed in Racak?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me more.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the Milosevic trial when I gave evidence. In the indictment he was also accused of being responsible for the death of 45 persons in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever resolve that mystery later?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During my testimony with the Trial Chamber and assisted by the Prosecutor, we compared our respective lists and clarified the matter, and it was clarified in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How was that? Can you give us an account?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a list of 40 persons who were identified. We compared that to the list of persons as included in the indictment and then we saw that the indictment contained nine more than were on my list. And then we compared and found out that some persons were mentioned twice, with the same name, and so we reduced the number to 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will have to ask you once more, after receiving the expert report of the pathologists or forensic medical expert, and I'm referring here to domestic experts, Dr. Dunjic, Dr. Dobricanin and others, and some colleagues from Belarus and later on they were joined by a Finnish forensic team headed by Dr. Helena Ranta. Do these reports mention a decapitated body of a man; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no decapitated body was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you found the bodies in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to establish from where the bodies had been taken to the mosque and who did that? Were there persons with who you could try to establish that at the site?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the site there was no one to help me establish that because none of the inhabitants of Racak were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, the very fact that you saw the clips that Ms. Gopalan showed you, and we keep speaking about document P1575 marked for identification, what did the fact that yesterday you saw those bodies which you claimed you couldn't recognise mean to you as an investigating judge? If those bodies were taken to the mosque later, what would that mean to you as an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would mean that everything that was found at the site was the result of manipulation. If the bodies were taken from the gully to the mosque, then much evidence that would be important for the subsequent investigation would have been destroyed. The body that we saw just now, the man who was wounded in the head but his cap remained on his head, then really I don't understand how he was wounded and how that body got there. And we saw a body and KLA soldiers and Walker pass that body by and nobody heeds it. And we also saw some other dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will not deal with this topic any further. My following questions are of a general nature and refer to newspaper articles. Yesterday my colleague referred to an article from the "Financial Times" and to an article from "Nin." There were statements given by various people from Mr. Destan Rukiqi to Dr. Flore Brovina to Natasha Kandic. Here's what I'm interested to hear. After these conflicts ended, did anybody launch any sort of proceedings against you on the grounds of the allegations that you were incriminated with in the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone from the official bodies call you ever to inquire about any potential incorrect conduct towards the citizens?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I resumed my normal duties with the district court in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe everyone in the courtroom will be pleased to hear that this closes my redirect. I wanted to thank the witness who came here to clarify many an issue that to this Defence team is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to hear a little bit more about the mosque you entered when you saw the 40 bodies. Could you describe the building when you entered, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day when we entered Racak, the mosque appeared undamaged. It looked like any other mosque in terms of structure. It was surrounded by a wall. As one enters the village and moves towards the centre it is on the right-hand side. It is circular, has many windows and a large open door. We entered the mosque. With me were all the team members as well as the OSCE representatives and the journalists who were there both domestic and foreign, with cameras. At a certain point in time, I allowed them to record the corpses. I'm trying to say that we all saw the corpses at the same moment. As I said, the mosque is a circular building, and the corpses were lined up in a circular fashion. Their heads were towards the windows and their feet was the centre of the mosque. They were dressed, and their faces were covered with something that resembled white towels. The first thing I did was to tell my scene-of-crime officer to assign numbers to each and every corpse because this is standard procedure. Each corpse had to be tagged, and when the journalists were recording, the forensic expert, Dr. Dobricanin, followed me from one corpse to the next. He uncovered each of the corpses to see the head, and we were mainly interested in seeing whether there were any visible injuries to the heads and whether there was any blood. We all saw it at the same time, it was all recorded. After that the journalists left and we resumed our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was it who entered the mosque first, you or who was it?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the first and then I was followed by everyone else. However, since the door was large and open, we all came in at the same time. The rest of the people there asked me whether they could enter and I said that we should all go in. The team members, the expert, the verifiers, and the journalists. It's all on the footage. There's a CD of that footage and you can see it all very well. It was shown in the Milosevic case when I testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many people altogether?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how many people, how many corpses were there in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. I know you testified there were 40 corpses, but how many people entered the mosque at the same time? How many in this group?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am afraid I can't be precise. In any case, the on-site investigation team members, the prosecutor, the forensic expert, the three representatives plus their interpreter, and there were journalists, perhaps five or six, so I would say anywhere between 10 and 15. I really didn't pay much attention to the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who touched the bodies? Who was really dealing with the corpses at that time?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one touched the bodies save for the expert. He didn't even touch them, but he simply picked up the towel to see the head and then he would put it back. No one else touched the bodies, and I didn't allow anyone to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you personally see despite of the faces or the heads anything else of the bodies, only the clothes of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have said so. They were all dressed in pants and jackets as well as vests and shoes. What I was able to observe that most of the corpses had thick soldiers pants as well as army boots and something that resembled army belts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you describe the clothes, especially the trousers and the vests in a little bit more detail?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had woolen sweaters, jackets, and track suits. As for the pants, they had the thick pants the army used to have. There may have been some with regular pants or bottom parts of track suits, but it was particularly interesting for me to see that some had what seemed to be military items of clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which colour?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Navy blue and dark grey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you describe the clothes of the female body?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I really cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't stay in the mosque for a long time. After we checked the bodies, everyone left the mosque, save for the scene of crime officers. In front of the mosque, there had already been a cistern or a reservoir truck parked. There were some workers there who were in charge of placing each corpse in a separate body-bag. The body-bags were sealed after which the corpses were put on to the truck. As a matter of fact, it was a refrigerator truck. In the presence of the verifiers, I ordered that the truck be sealed and that it was not to be touched until we returned from the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm interested in the concrete work and the duty of Dr. Dobricanin. What exactly did he when he was in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dobricanin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he looked at each corpse individually. He would raise the towel, check the head, comment on something, and he put it back. That's all he could do at that time as a doctor, a forensic medical expert, that's all he could do at that moment to offer what he could immediately observe. This was not an official examination. He merely wanted to check what we were interested in the most, and that is to see whether there were any traces of slaughter on those bodies that could be determined visually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means he didn't turn the bodies to the other side, upside down, or investigated the heads of the bodies? He just looked at them? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When he -- he looked at every and each of these 40 bodies as you told us, and then you heard his comment that he stated loud that there were no trace of any slaughter on those bodies, and this way it is recorded what you said yesterday. Have you an estimation between the beginning of his investigation to this comment?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Time-wise I don't know how long it lasted, but he made the full round of the bodies, and he commented on it, and it was all recorded. You can hear it for yourselves. You can hear him say those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, I should like to take you back to your evidence touching Gornje Obrinje very briefly. Now, you testified that the district court in Pristina had received a request from a number of families who lived in Gornje Obrinje? And they had reported that some of the family members who had been killed were actually buried in Gornje Obrinje; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the information we had. We were not able to verify it though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you get any idea at all as to how many bodies there were buried there?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, in their request they did not specify any numbers. Perhaps they didn't know it either. We tried to ascertain that and in order to do so, all the bodies found needed to be exhumed and autopsied. This was all supposed to have been done on the spot, hence I am afraid I cannot estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You never did get that number. But tell me now, in answer to Ms. Gopalan, you stated that the on-site investigation was never completed because you were prevented from attending the scene. I think Helena Ranta you said told you that there were KLA blockades and there was a conversation between you and Ms. Ranta. And you said, for objective reasons, the investigation could not have been completed.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Well, now, you testified that in Racak you were prevented from carrying out the on-site investigation on three occasions. You went first on the 15th and you were shot at and you had to return to Stimlje. And notwithstanding that danger, you returned on the 16th, and again you were shot at, and you had to return to Stimlje. And you went again on the 17th and again you were shot at, and it was only on the 18th that you were able to carry out that investigation in Racak. Now, my question to you, Mrs. Marinkovic, is this: Having been prevented from attending the scene at Gornje Obrinje on one occasion, why did you not return a second or a third time as you did in Racak? Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was no goodwill on the part of the Finnish team to do this jointly. They actually tried to steer clear of us avoiding any further contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So is it that the investigation depended on the Finnish team to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't depend on the Finnish team, but given that it was on the level of the court and the prosecutor's office as well as the Finnish team, there had been a meeting, they agreed upon doing this jointly. Therefore, I had no further influence on that. This was decided upon on a level senior to mine to go there the next day. Helena Ranta herself said that there were terrorists, that there were KLA in Gornje Obrinje and that we wouldn't be able to conduct an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So as far as you can tell us, you never conducted an investigation into the killing and burial of those persons, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't. Someone else might have. Since I didn't do it, it didn't necessarily have to mean that no one else could. I really don't know whether there was an on-site investigation and whether it was ever completed. On the day I wanted to go, it wasn't, but I don't know whether it was followed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But for somebody else to have done that, what would have had to happen? Would there have to be fresh requests? Would Ms. Ranta have to come in? What would have to happen?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the family asked for it to be done, if it was in their interest, then the president was supposed to decide on it and to assign it to me or someone else. This was just a single investigative measure depending on the fact who was on duty at any given point in time and who was there to conduct an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: And this leads me now to another question, Mrs. Marinkovic, you stated that the families were no longer requesting any investigations, and my question is, the families having made the first request for an investigation into the killing and burying of their family members, was it necessary for them to make further and continuous requests for that investigation to continue on, or could that one request have been sufficient?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that request was submitted by the families of the victims. We, in such case, act urgently following the receipt of such a request filed by the families of victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes. But you said that one of the reasons why you didn't pursue the investigation was because the families were no longer requesting any investigations, and my question to you is, was it necessary for them to continue requesting, having made the first request?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain that. When we act upon a request, it is on their request that we take any further steps. They didn't come to see me subsequently. They may have turned to the court, maybe the court president assigned it to someone else. I don't know what the final outcome concerning the Gornje Obrinje incident was. I only know that on that day we wanted to go there in order to complete it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. What time did you and the team set out from Pristina for Gornje Obrinje? Do you recollect the time roughly?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we set out around 6.00 a.m. from Pristina. I know it was early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Okay. As best you can, I know it may be a bit difficult, but can you tell me, can you tell us, who comprised that team that you set out with from Pristina? Roughly how many?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Standard members of an on-site investigation: Myself, the district prosecutor, a court forensic expert, Mr. Dobricanin and his assistant Dr. Susanna, I can't recall her last name. From the Finnish team, there was Helena Ranta, the ambassador for human rights whose name I can't recall with his wife, and two or three other persons. I know in any case that there were two full OSCE vehicles. There was our vehicle and a column of policemen who were there to accompany us and to secure the scene. I don't know how many of them there were. At the head of the column, there were OSCE representatives since they had visited the scene once before without us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, how long would it have taken you, had you not been stopped by Ms. Ranta. Roughly how long would it have taken you to get from Prishtina to Gornje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we travelled quite a long time from Pristina to -- I think we were halfway to Gornje Obrinje when we stopped. I really can't recall how long it took us. In any case, we stopped in the middle of the main road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, now, that was when you and Ms. Ranta had the conversation about her wanting you to go along and you wanted to have the police escort.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they stopped suddenly. We didn't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You said that. And you came out of the vehicle and then you and Ms. Ranta spoke. Now, the important thing, though, Mrs. Marinkovic, is that you say it was getting dark around that time?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during the winter, so after 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. it's already dark. I don't know how long we stayed there. And the first moment I thought they wanted to get some rest and that's why they had stopped and then I started speaking with Helena. Then the ambassador's wife when she realised the turn that conversation was taking, she couldn't say anything but put her hands together and she said, Madam, please, no. She was signalling to me not to go any further. I'll never forget that. And then we realised that up on the hills they had already started surrounding us in black uniforms slouched with automatic rifles. They were setting up ambush. I've also explained the conversation I had with Helena Ranta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: If it were getting dark, Mrs. Marinkovic, by the time you got to Gornje Obrinje, had you not been stopped, it would have been dark, so how would you have carried out the exhumation in the darkness?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we would not have arrived there during the dark. We stayed quite a long time in the road explaining, discussing. Our plan was to get there between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m. As Helena had told us, the alleged mass grave was as one enters the village. That's the information they had. Had we been able to reach that location, we would have been able to complete it during daylight. We simply exhume the bodies, we take samples, and then the rest including autopsies is done at the forensic medical institute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there's just one last question, Mrs. Marinkovic, and I shall relieve you. I want to hear your comments on a matter. Now, you stated that during the investigation the investigating judges, the only person authorised to collect evidence? Yes?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: And you also said that some investigative activities the investigating judge would transfer to the police, for example, an order to search certain facilities if necessary, to locate the perpetrator of crime or objects that were used in committing crime.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these investigative measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: And you answered Mr. Djordjevic that the police cannot ask questions or have demands towards the investigating judge or even issue orders?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, can I have your comment on this statement, Mrs. Marinkovic. MUP officials could institute investigations when the urgency of the situation required it, and they were not hampered by the presence or absence of the investigative judge or the prosecutor. What comment would you have on that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, colleague, let me tell you, that was in force during the state of war because a decree had been passed by the federal government about the application of the war [as interpreted] on criminal procedure in the state of war, so while the state of war was in force, the investigating judge and police bodies could conduct an investigation without a request made by the public prosecutor if that was urgent. But the investigating judge and the MUP were duty-bound to immediately inform the public prosecutor. But that applied only in the state of war because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Did it ever happen? Did you ever experience it at all?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I wasn't faced with such a situation. The public prosecutor always acted in a timely fashion, and I always carried out their request. There was no case where I had to conduct an investigation urgently and directly with that request by the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I thank you very much indeed, and I apologise for keeping you that long. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and for the assistance that you've been able to give over several days. You are, of course, now, able to return to your normal activities and a Court Officer will assist you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Trial Chamber for your tolerance and understanding. Some of my answers may have been long, but it was only because I tried to help to find the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz, I still have one or two evidentiary matters from the last witness. Are you moving on?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, no, no, I actually wanted to raise just a housekeeping matter concerning exhibits that relate to this witness, Ms. Marinkovic, before we move on to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's where I was wanting to go. So you do yours first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday during the course of cross-examination, Ms. Gopalan referred to an exhibit. This is 06078, and it's a complaint by Fazli Balaj, the Defence lawyer Isak Aliu. This was dealt with at transcript page 13029. We intended to tender this exhibit yesterday, but just due to an oversight it wasn't tendered at the time, so I move to tender this exhibit at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't risen to object. The reason why I rise is to point out that Ms. Gopalan showed the Trial Chamber and the parties this document, and we are not opposed to it being admitted. It was shown on the screen immediately before a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will therefore be received as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P01579, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have three other exhibits, and these are exhibits that were tendered through during the testimony of Mrs. Marinkovic in the Milutinovic case. They have not been used during her testimony in this case, but for the sake of completeness of the record and since the testimony has been tendered by the Defence, we seek to tender those exhibits, and I can -- they are just three of them. I can read out the 65 ter number and indicate the transcript page in the Milutinovic case where each one is referred to, if that pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lack understanding for this, and the Defence objects because Ms. Gopalan could have shown this document during the cross-examination. I believe that this is contrary to the rules and, therefore, we oppose the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you may have misunderstood what is proposed. These are each documents that are -- were exhibited in the course of the trial in the Milutinovic case. They were documents put to this witness who then commented on them. You have tendered the transcript. The Prosecution says, well, you ought to -- if you want to understand parts of the transcript, you need to see the documents that the witness was talking about, so it's really to fill out the transcript that you have tendered that I understand these three exhibits are offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there has been an identical situation and yet the Trial Chamber failed to show understanding. Of course, it's up to the Bench to decide, but we persist in opposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can recall many occasions when exhibits that were referred to in transcripts tendered both by the Defence and the Prosecution have been received in evidence so that the tendered transcript can be better understood. So pursuing our consistent practice, we will receive these three exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll proceed to read out the 65 ter numbers. The first one is 03109, and in the Milutinovic case this was Exhibit P3109, and it's referred to at transcript page 23597. And I ask that that exhibit be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit P01580. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 65 ter 03106. In the Milutinovic case this was P3106. And it's referred to at transcript page 23580 of the Milutinovic transcript. I ask that that exhibit be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P01581. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the last exhibit is 03095. In the Milutinovic case it was P3095, and it's referred to at transcript page 23562. And I ask that that exhibit be received. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number P01582. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is outstanding a matter of the admissibility of the video footage which is said to have been taken ... [Microphone not activated] ... on 16th of January, 1999 at Racak. The Prosecution has sought to tender this. The Defence has spoken briefly in opposition. The issue is concerning the admissibility of this are not short or simple. In the Chamber's view it would be appropriate to receive written submissions from both parties so that we can give proper consideration to the concerns expressed against the admission so that we would ask that within by Wednesday of next week, if that is not unreasonable, submissions be received from both Prosecution and Defence in the hope that we can deal with that matter and reach a decision before we break for the Easter break. Was there any other evidentiary matter left unresolved in the course of the evidence of the last witness? We are not aware of any. Just checking. Very well. That concludes that phase. I believe the next witness may be waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Djurdjic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please state for the transcript your personal information.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I am Vukasin Jokanovic. I was born on the 18th of November, 1939, in the village of Gornje Slatina, municipality Vitina in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of law in Skopje, Macedonia. I worked as a lawyer, and currently I am a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly tell us the main points of your biography?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from university, I found a job at the tobacco factory in Gnjilane. I worked there as a lawyer. After that, I worked at a medical centre, also as a lawyer. In 1969, I was elected member of the Municipal Assembly of Gnjilane. And in 1970 in April, I was elected president of the Municipal Assembly of Gnjilane. I stayed in that position for two terms of office, four years each, that is a total of eight years. After that, I was elected by the Provincial Assembly of Kosovo to be a member of the executive committee of Kosovo, and at the same time I was a provincial secretary for legislation and general administration. I stayed in that position for four years. After that I was elected to be a member of the provincial committee of the league of communists of Kosovo. I was one of several executive secretaries in the dealing with the issues of the political system and legal matters. The Provincial Assembly of Kosovo also elected me a member of the presidency of Kosovo. That was the highest ranking government body in Kosovo, in the province of Kosovo. I stayed in that position until 1988, early 1998, after which I was elected president of the Provincial Assembly of Kosovo. I remained in that position for two terms in office, each term of one year. So I stayed there throughout 1988 and 1989. In late 1989 there were elections, and I was elected a member of the Republican Assembly of Serbia from Kosovo for the constituency of Gnjilane. So I was a member of Serbian parliament and vice-president of parliament of Serbia. After that I was member of parliament of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was a truncated Yugoslavia which consisted only of Serbia and Montenegro. In 1995, as far as I remember, I was elected member of the cabinet, the federal cabinet of truncated Yugoslavia. Apart from that, I was also minister of the interior. I stayed in that position for three years. After that the president of Yugoslavia, Zoran Lilic, and the president of Montenegro as well as the president of Serbia proposed that I be appointed state public prosecutor of Yugoslavia, and I remained in that position for four years until the end of my term in office, and then I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that most of your working career you spent in Kosovo and Metohija. I would like to hear about the development of the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I mostly worked on matters that had to do with that. After Yugoslavia was created after the Second World War, the province was an autonomous region by the name of Kosovo and Metohija, whereas Vojvodina was a province. Later in 1963, Kosovo began to be called a province like Vojvodina. In the previous period, the highest-ranking legal act was its statute, but under the new constitution as of 1963, the highest-ranking legal act was the constitutional law. What followed were the amendments in 1969, 1970, 1971, when the province received greater powers. And under those amendments it was a province that was a constituent part of the Republic of Serbia, but simultaneously it was a constituent element of Yugoslavia. That position was reinforced by the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when you were first faced with Albanian separatist demands?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally was faced with Albanian separatist demands in 1968 in Gnjilane for the first time. I worked and lived there at the time. On the 27th of November, there were demonstrations. They started off from the secondary school centre. That's a part of town where all the secondary schools were. They started walking down the main street all the way to the other end of town where they dispersed. They were shouting out slogans like "Kosovo republic" for the most part, and "unification."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can add that these demonstrations were a huge surprise to us who lived in Gnjilane at the time, but even beyond Gnjilane because Yugoslavia was very well organised at the time and so was the League of Communists, and that was a shock to many citizens and to everybody who supported the communist system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the goal of these demonstrations was?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe the goal was or the aim was what you could tell from the slogans, namely, that the province receive the status of a republic, so that it be transformed from a province to a republic. And the second slogan, "unification" I understood to mean the unification of territories inhabited by Albanians. So if a province becomes a republic, it practically becomes a state as part of the SFRY which was also a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, that slogan "Kosovo republic" what did it mean politically and legally?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It meant that the constitutional system in force was being validated. And these demonstrations were assessed as hostile demonstrations because they were undermining the legal system, undermining the equality, brotherhood and unity, all the values that were especially upheld at the time. And such demonstrations took place not only in Gnjilane, but also in Urosevac at that time. But also in Pristina, and I know that there were such demonstrations in Tetovo Macedonia, too, where the ethnic Albanians are the majority population. The demonstrations were held on the eve of an Albanian public holiday, the 28th of November. Some call it flag day, but it's actually an Albanian national holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the difference between the status of an autonomous province and that of a republic at the time of these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was an essential difference. The republics were states with their borders and Yugoslavia as a state also had its borders. Whereas, the provinces were parts of Serbia and they were social political communities. That was the official term. So they didn't have a stronger status than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were the consequences of these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the inter-ethnic relations suffered most gravely from that because tensions arose, and there was concern that the process that started might be continued. I remember my father telling me, well, this isn't all we've seen of it, this is going to spread. I was young at the time and didn't believe him, but later I saw that it did spread indeed. So inter-ethnic relations deteriorated and the process of leaving Kosovo to relocate to other parts of Serbia began.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we have reached the time when we must have the break. I'm sorry, we must interrupt your evidence at this point, but our tapes must be rewound. Because of another matter, we may be five or so minutes late in returning. So we'll aim for 20 minutes past 4.00. We'll have a break. A Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, a moment ago you told us that in 1974 a new constitution of the SFRY was proclaimed as well as the constitutions of Serbia and the Autonomous Province of Kosovo. By virtue of the new SFRY constitution, what was the status of the province?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The SFRY constitution clearly prescribed that Yugoslavia consisted of six republics, and that in one of the republics, i.e., Serbia, there were two provinces. These being Vojvodina and Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document -- Defence document D011-4638. Your Honours, could we be allowed to provide the witness with a binder of documents in hard copy so as to speed things up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic, but can we make clear now that we are content to receive a quick and general introduction to the previous history but you will appreciate our concern in this indictment commences in 1999. We do not want to spend a long time learning detail of matters that are not going to assist us in our decision. I mention that now because if you are going to a large bundle of documents, it may be the case that a number of them are not really relevant to the materials in this case. So we ask you to bear that in mind as you deal with the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't have a great deal of documents. It is our intention to indicate the basic elements concerning the status of the autonomous province within the Federation constitutionally and legally speaking. We heard several witnesses testify about the removal of certain powers from the autonomous province and the causes of what ensued. I intended to go through these documents in a general fashion only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are grateful for that. Please keep it strongly in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we first have page 31. Now that we can see that this was the constitution. Can we go to page 31, Article 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, please provide us with brief comments of Articles 1 and 2 bearing in mind of what you have just explained to us.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Article 1, the basis of that article is, without going through all of it, that the SFRY was a federal state of different peoples and United Nations in the form of socialist republics and socialist Autonomous Provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo, which were constituent parts of the socialist Republic of Serbia. That was the basis. As for Article 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on Article 3?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Article 2 or 3?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Each republic is a state based on the sovereignty of the people. This is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Article 4, what does that prescribe?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It states that the socialist autonomous provinces are social political communities. This stresses the difference between a republic and a socio-political community.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Briefly, Article 5.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The territories are those of the republics, and they are not to be changed without the consent of the republic in question. The same goes for the territory of the autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the following two articles, who has borders?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavia and the republics. This is not a happenstance, this is the constitutional terminology put in there to underline the difference between the republics and provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 212 in the English. That is Article 321 of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you comment briefly on this article by virtue of which the Presidency of the SFRY ...

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The briefest comment I can provide is that the most senior organ in the Yugoslavia is the Presidency. That is to say, the collective presidential institution comprising one member from each of the republics and one member from each of the provinces who are to be elected by members of the republican and provincial Assemblies. By secret ballot, by all those present. In this most senior Yugoslavian body, there was equal representation of all republics and provinces amounting to one representative each.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the Assembly of the SFRY how many committees and councils were there, and what was the representation of republics and provinces?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the SFRY had the federal council, and in each -- there were 30 deputies from each republic, and the provinces had 20 in it. The second council was the council of the republics and provinces in which the republics had 12 deputies each and the provinces 8. This was to serve to stress the difference between the republics and provinces in terms of numbers. In essence, this did not impact the decision-making process because consensus was pursued in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 194 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is Article 291 and 292.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these articles prescribe the composition of the councils of the Chambers, both of which have been explained by the witness. I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00902. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D130.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 2. We are about to see the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia from 1974. Can you tell us briefly what was the status of the autonomous provinces according to this constitution?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't read it from the screen. Can you please zoom in. In any case, I think that the constitution of the Republic of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 16 in the English and Article 1 in the Serbian. Page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your binder, you have Article 1.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Of the Serbian constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me see what page that is. Yes, I found it. Article 1. The basic thing here is that the Socialist Republic of Serbia is a state of the Serbian people and other nations and nationalities. The next article states that, the next paragraph states that Serbia comprises the Autonomous Provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo, as well as that the Socialist Republic of Serbia shall be a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 17 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is your Article 3.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The territory of the republic shall comprise the territories of the municipalities as envisaged by the law. The borders of the republic may be changed only on the basis of a decision by the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. The borders were key and each and every change had to be decided on by the Assembly. That's the gist of this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 99 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Article 291 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Chapter 8, socialist autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is copied from the Yugoslav constitution stating that the provinces were socio-political communities in which the nations and nationalities exercised their sovereign rights except for those rights in the common interests of the working people, citizens, nations and nationalities of the republic as a whole. Such rights could only be exercised within the republic as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we next please go to page 104 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Article 300 in your binder. Just a brief comment, please.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Article 300 is the only article in the Serbian constitution which enumerates the issues which may be applied uniformly across the territory of the Republic of Serbia including the two provinces. Such issues and laws pertaining to them are valid in the territory of the entire republic. No other issues could be regulated by the republic save for those enumerated in here. There were many problems concerning this article, which I worked on as well. Among other things, it envisaged the regulation of principles, basic principles, as you can see in the items enumerated. In legal interpretation, this posed many difficulties in the sense of what is the concept and boundaries of a principle, a basic principle. There was much discussion to come up with a universally accepted language of this constitution. I was the secretary of the province, and I know that in the technical legal process, there were many problems in how to interpret the notion of principles, basic principles, et cetera. Basically all matters which were not strictly prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How were the delegates from the province of Kosovo represented in the bodies of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the Republic of Serbia, the autonomous provinces were represented in the same way as any other part of Serbia's territory. It depended on the population, the ethnic makeup, the number of municipalities, and the number of workers because there were three chambers. The provinces were represented in the Republic of Serbia in such a way that Kosovo had its delegates. The number who are dependent on the population, but there were three chambers, and one chamber was the chamber of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did the delegates in Kosovo and Metohija take part in the election of the Serbian member of the federal Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The delegates from Kosovo as well as those from Vojvodina were on an equal footing with the other delegates from other parts of Serbia or Serbia proper as it was called in the political lingo. They took part in the elections for all structures, bodies, judges, in the legislative process and in all matters about which the Assembly decided. So all delegates from provinces or not took part in the decision-making process on an equal footing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 125 of the English version and Article 361 of the Serbian original. That is page 125 of the English version. And Article 361 in the Serbian version. Let's just wait for it to appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Here we can see the composition of the Presidency of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that is Article 361. 364 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. It's actually 364 on page 125.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It has 15 members, they are elected by the Assembly of Serbia, as I said, and by virtue of their position, the Presidency shall include the president of the Assembly of the SRS, the president of the central committee of the League of Communists, and the presidents of the presidencies of the provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the members from the province as being members of the Presidency of Serbia. Did it apply vice-versa?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no representatives of other parts of Serbia in the Presidency of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D011-5078. Your Honours, I wish to inform you that the translation of this document is pending so we don't have an English version yet. It is just the basic provisions upon which I would like to ask the witness to comment. This is the constitution of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo, so with the Chamber's leave, I would like to have this marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00903 marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, please give us a brief comment on Article 1 of the constitution of the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The constitutions of Yugoslavia, of Serbia, and of Kosovo are interconnected and many provisions are harmonised. This Article 1 defines the province of Kosovo, and as of 1974, the province of Kosovo has had a constitution. Until that time it only had a constitutional law as the highest legal act. The province is a socio-political community of Albanians, Serbs, Turks, and Montenegrins. This was an issue whether a strong presence in political life and, therefore, it wasn't possible to treat the province as a province of Albanians but rather as a province of the peoples and nationalities listed here in an alphabetic order. In one linguistic version it's Albanians, Muslims, et cetera, and in the other linguistic version the sequence is difference, the Albanians are mentioned last because in the Albanian language the word for Albanian is Siptar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This also includes the provision from the constitution of Serbia stipulating that the province of Kosovo is an integral part of the Republic of Serbia and of the Federation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a brief comment of Article 4?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Article 4. The territory of the province shall consist of the territories of the municipalities. And the province of -- the territory of the province of Kosovo cannot be changed without the approval of the provincial Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about Article 4?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Article 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And Article 5, please, too.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they speak about equality, which is the starting point of all constitutions, that is all citizens have the same rights and duties. And Article 5 specifically speaks about the equality of languages. That is the constitution of Kosovo, autonomously regulates the equality of the Albanian, Serbian, and Turkish languages and their respective scripts, and that is then regulated by the province which sees to it that this principle is applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a brief look at Article 301, paragraph 1, please.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Of the constitution of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the powers of the Assembly, what the Assembly can regulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm only interested in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly of Kosovo decides about any amendments to the constitution of the province of Kosovo. That is, paragraph 1 gives the right to the province to decide autonomously about the constitution of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo. It decides about amendments to the constitution, yes. And that at the same time it gives its approval to, and this is very important, its approval to amendments to the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Republic of Serbia. That is, the province has such strong rights that without its approval neither the constitution of Serbia nor the constitution of Yugoslavia can be amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did the bodies of Yugoslavia and the government bodies of Serbia give their approval for the amendment of the constitution of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The province was autonomous here, but its constitution had to be harmonised with these other constitutions of Serbia and that of Yugoslavia. But there was no such participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you now please go to Article 301, paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly of Kosovo shall elect a member of the Presidency of the Yugoslavia. That is, its own member, one of a total of eight members. And the Assembly of the province of Kosovo elects and the members of its own Presidency, because Kosovo had its Presidency and Serbia had its own and Yugoslavia had its own Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already had this document marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please tell me now what the ethnic makeup of the government bodies of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo was like?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The government bodies of the province of Kosovo had an ethnic makeup which on the whole reflected the ethnic makeup of the population. That ethnic makeup or we called it the key in our political jargon was also applied to all other administrative bodies and to a certain extent also in the economy, and this was also applied to municipal structures. Depending on the ethnic make up, we strove to see that all ethnic communities be proportionally represented. And as the percentage of Albanians was about 70 per cent, we can see that in the bodies of the province, the Albanians made up 70 per cent of the composition. Whereas, the Serbs, Turks, Montenegrins took part with their respective shares.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How did Kosovo and Metohija develop in the 1970s and 1980s?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As I lived and worked in Kosovo for the most part of my career, starting from 1970 we witnessed rapid socio-economic development, which made possible the establishment of a special fund at Yugoslav level which was called, the fund for the development of the underdeveloped and Kosovo. The province of Kosovo played an important part in that fund. From that fund various economic operators were funded or health care, et cetera, so the funds from this fund were used for development and for the raising of the cultural educational level to a higher degree. And as an immediate participant, I can say that Kosovo within a brief time-period made such a leap in development for which other peoples or nations needed decades. But owing to this fund to which all republics contributed, such rapid social and economic development became possible. We often stressed that in our political work and in our political speeches. At the federal level, at the level of the republic, and also at the level of the province. We also gave examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the situation in education and science?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Education also expanded greatly. Many schools were built. More pupils started attending schools, both primary and secondary, and then some faculties were established. First they were organisationally part of the university of Belgrade, but soon the university of Pristina was established, which grew rapidly, and it became the third largest university in Yugoslavia exceeded only by Zagreb and Belgrade, and this applied to the number of students and to the number of faculties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were national academies founded?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Once the number of scientists had grown and science had developed there were doctors of science and then the Kosovo academy of sciences of arts was founded, what included an institute called the Albanological institute. It studied the history of the Albanian nationality, its culture, et cetera, and that's why it was called the Albanological institute. There was also an academy of sciences, and such academies were found in Vojvodina and in other parts, that is republics, of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with the infrastructure like?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Kosovo was the least developed region and infrastructure was poorly developed. But owing to the aid provided by the working class and the working people of the entire country who contributed from their salaries, a large number of facilities was built. Roads, irrigation systems, as well as other public utilities that improved the quality of life in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in the early 1980s were there demonstrations and how did they come about?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1981 there were large demonstrations in Kosovo. They started in March. I remember the exact date, it was the 11th of March, because anniversaries have been celebrated since. And they lasted until early April. These demonstrations started in the students centre, that is in the students cafeteria, and they went on until the 3rd or 4th of April with some interruptions, and they grew day by day. These were very serious large demonstrations that also had a destructive element, and there were serious clashes with the police. And these demonstrations were the focus of many activities, and they were much discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What triggered these demonstrations, and what were the demonstrators demands?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The first time when the students gathered in the students mess, the initial request concerned food, but once they were out in the street, we began seeing the same slogans we had seen back in 1968. The basic one was "Kosovo republic" and "unification." The largest demonstrations took place in early April in Pristina, but there were demonstrations in other cities and towns as well. Many citizens from other towns came to Pristina and joined the demonstrations so the state authorities were not able to suppress those demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the nature of those demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: They were used by the various political foray in Kosovo, rather, they were seen as hostile aiming at undermining the constitution and territorial integrity of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were these peaceful demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on everything I said, they were not. They were quite violent actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who reacted to them and how?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The first ones to react were the security organs and the police of Kosovo. They were unable to suppress them. Next, Serbian organs offered assistance to their colleagues in Kosovo, however, the leaders in Kosovo did not allow for that. The organs of Serbian police were prevented from entering in the municipality of Kursumlija at the border crossing. This created additional problems and a compromise was reached. So-called joint security forces were created comprising members from all the Yugoslav Republics and from the province of Vojvodina. It was then that Serbian forces were allowed to participate as part of that joint force and allowed to enter Kosovo in order to assist in the suppression of the demonstrations. Those joint forces remained in Kosovo until 1990. Given that the demonstrations were very violent and involved great -- a great many people, the army intervened as well following a request made by the committee for the defence of Kosovo. The army arrived from Skopje, Macedonia. It was a tank unit. In order to protect all key facilities in the province. The provincial Assembly, the chamber, the banks, and radio and TV stations. The joint forces were trying to keep law and order. These demonstrations were the cause for a state of emergency in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who were the sending parties to the joint forces followed by the request of the counsel for the defence of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The federal government did through its federal interior ministry with the previous agreement of all the republics. The commander of the joint forces was from Croatian. I think he was Croatian. As part of the joint forces there was a special unit commanded by Slovenia. The joint forces had their staff and were located in different towns and cities in Kosovo. Their staff was in Pristina and in Avajlija and the environs of Pristina. The forces were deployed in such a way that, for example, in Vitina where I hail from, there were Croatian police forces in addition to the Kosovo ones. In Urosevac there were policemen from Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the Army of Yugoslavia. Did it participate in the suppression of the demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia was there to flex the muscle, to put a show of force. The tanks arrived from Skopje to Pristina down the main street in order to demonstrate its power. Pristina also saw sorties of the Yugoslav air force. Their goal of which was to have a psychological impact on those participating in the demonstrations, as well as on the citizens in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D011-4952.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 4. Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I kept this in my personal archive. This is an official pass. Because of the state of emergency, one could not move about freely in Pristina. At the time, I was a member of the Executive Council and even I could not move about freely. I couldn't even go to work without a pass such as this. It is clearly stated here why it was issued. It says that it was issued for the person in question to be allowed to move freely. It was drafted in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit Number D00904. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were the consequences of the 1981 demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Given their scope and nature, as well as their slogans and numbers of those involved, all that had a very negative impact on the political situation and inter-ethnic relations in Kosovo. A very unfavourable climate was created, raising concerns with all those who wanted to live in Yugoslavia and under the social political system as existed at the time. This concern was shared by all the ethnicities.
