However, there was growing insecurity, lack of trust, and fear of the future because during the demonstrations as well as afterwards, there were different attacks, individuals were attacked as well as their property. All this had a grave impact on the inter-ethnic relations which resulted in an increasing number of Serbs and Montenegrins moving out of Kosovo in numbers greater than they had been after the demonstrations in 1968. The inter-ethnic relations worsened by far, and all this was contrary to the existing policies and political system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of the republican state organs vis-a-vis the resolution of the Kosovo problem?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The problem was spotted relatively early on in the federal institutions, Serbian institutions, as well as in Kosovo itself. The party bodies as well as Assembly bodies from the state down to the province and municipalities issued programmes in order to stop this tendency of emigrating and trying to return those who had already moved away. This problem was dealt with by the Yugoslav Serbian provincial and municipal organs. There existed such the so-called Yugoslav programme for the return of those who had immigrated and to stop this trend.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned Pristina university, what was the ethnic makeup until 1981 and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The worsening inter-ethnic relations, the demonstrations, and the participation of Albanian students in the demonstrations caused great rifts at the university in particular. This raised concerns and introduced a feeling of insecurity among Serbian, Turkish, and other students. During that time, as far as I recall, according to the information the provincial bodies had, 60 per cent of all teaching staff who were not Albanians moved out of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like in rural areas?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There it was particularly pronounced because there was harassment, damage to crops, and threats to people's safety and property. There were also cases of physical attacks and even murders. I recall a number of murders which occurred during that period. A Sarkic was killed from the village of Mejic [phoen] near Malkovica [phoen]. I recall that in particular because I was among others tasked by the president of the Presidency of Kosovo to investigate it. This Sarkic person had complained in written form, and he had foreseen his fate in a way. He believed he would eventually be killed. People didn't believe him at first, and we went to talk to the authorities in Djakovica and went to his family home. I had information which indicated that there had been shots fired at his house. It was actually before he was killed. At that point in time he expressed his grave concern that he would be killed and the Djakovica authorities promised to assist him. Unfortunately, a little while later, he was killed indeed. I was badly shaken up because I was involved in trying to help him. There was another family where the father and son were killed in Samodreza. I also remember the Martinovic case, but there were many other attacks and cases which raised concerns and caused fear among the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the situation like in terms of the functioning of the Republic of Serbia in its exercise of its powers across the territory?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: By virtue of the 1974 constitution, the republic could exercise all of its functions and powers across the territory. I tried to illustrate that by telling you that the Serbian policemen could not enter the province on their own without previously consulting the federal organs. In all matters internal, it was the provincial organs who were in charge of regulating the situation. Effectively the Serbian authorities exercised their power only in Serbia proper. As for the implementation of all provincial laws and regulation, it was the provincial organs that were tasked with implementing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when were the first steps taken in order to overcome this problem of functioning, and how was it resolved?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After the first set of amendments was proclaimed by which the province received broadened powers and after the constitution in -- demonstrations after 1968, there were people in Kosovo who were opposed to such processes, including Jova Sotra, Misa Sekulovic [phoen], Jevica Pecinovic [phoen]. I recall them in particular because they were kicked out of the League of Communists, and they actually moved since they were left without work. One of them, Mr. Sotra, died soon afterwards. There was opposition to the changes which were made to the constitution in 1974. In the Republic of Serbia I seem to remember the existence of something called the Blue Book in which I analysed the constitutional status of Serbia. It was quickly set aside, but after 1981 and after all the events I have been discussing, it became topical again because it became clear that the Serbian constitution had to be changed in order for Serbia to regain its basic functions of statehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who reacted to the situation and how?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the situation with the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Formally speaking, the first initiative came from the Presidency of Serbia as the most senior body in Serbia. A group, a task force was formed presided over by the president of the Serbian Presidency, Mr. Ivan Stambolic. There were also two members, I believe it was Spiro Galovic, and I don't seem to recall the other one. There were also representatives from Vojvodina. I recall Vojadinovic [phoen], and there were representatives from Kosovo including myself and two Albanians who were constitutional experts. The force was tasked with drafting a plan of changes to the constitution in order to have it move in the direction desired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the results of the work of that task force of the Presidency of the SRS were?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a material that was sent to the Assembly of Serbia and the Assembly accepted it and tasked the constitutional commission of the Assembly to start drafting amendments to the constitution of Serbia based on that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the work continue after the Assembly made its decision?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The constitutional commission to be able to work on the amendments to the constitution established a smaller group which was shared by Bora Jovic, and they had a number of members from the constitutional commission of Serbia, and members of that group were also members from Kosovo and Vojvodina. They were also directly involved in drafting the language of the amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did the work on drafting the amendments begin, and how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It took three years. From 1986 until 1989. The work on the constitutional amendments and the harmonisation took all that time because the procedure was -- the process rather, was very complicated because we had a unique system not to be found elsewhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did these members of the constitutional commission have to harmonise their proposals with what was called the basis at the time?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a duty. The members from Vojvodina and those from Kosovo couldn't act on their own. They had to inform the official authorities of the province, above all the Presidency and the executive committee, and of course the League of Communists, because at the time the League of Communists had what was called the leading role in our society.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the essence of the amendments to the constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that the work took as much as three years, or rather, although it took three years, we agreed that we should only change issues regarding the functioning of the state, namely, matters that have to do with the security of the entire republic. Furthermore, matters connected with the people's defence of interest to the republic as a whole, and the constitutional remit of the Republic of Serbia. Can the Republic of Serbia adopt its constitution and can it do so independently, autonomously, and what the procedure is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did these amendments change the constitutional position of the province and its powers with regard to the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The constitutional position of the province in the Federation was not changed by these amendments. The rights of the province in the Federation remained intact. The province remained a constituent element of the Federation with all rights and duties stemming therefrom. With regard to the Republic of Serbia, the amendments changed the powers with of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll deal with that a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it's time for the technical break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is so, Mr. Djurdjic. We must break now. We resume at 6.00. It is too detailed and too long, if I could give you a summary of what is happening to date. So if you can think about that over the break. Thank you, we resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, when the constitutional commission of the Assembly of Serbia finished its work, what was the result?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The constitutional commission of the Assembly of Serbia submitted its proposed amendments to the Assembly of Serbia to adopt, which the Assembly of Serbia did and then a public discussion ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the results of the public discussion?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In our system, that public discussion was very broad. The constitutional amendments were discussed at all levels from villages to town neighbourhoods to all elected bodies, as well as professional and expert institutions, scientific institutes, especially legal -- organisations of legal scholars. I also took part in that discussion and there were the statements of the president of the socialist league which was a socio-protocol institution charged with moderating that discussion. And about 400.000 people took part in that discussion, whereas over 30.000 actually contributed to it actively.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the procedure after the public discussion?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After the public discussion all the comments and proposals were summarised, some were founded, others unfounded. Some were professionally relevant, others weren't. And all the most important matters are singled out and forwarded to the constitutional commission of Serbia to accept them or refuse, always giving an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who proposed the amendments to the constitution, to the constitutional commission of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The constitutional commission of Serbia which was the body in charge received the amendments from the socialist league.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did the constitutional commission adopt these amendments?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all three chambers of the Assembly of Serbia accepted these amendments, and these adopted amendments were also forwarded to the Assemblies of Vojvodina and Kosovo to give their approval to these amendments which was constitutional procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Before giving their approval to the amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, were there any events in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are. There was resistance to approving those amendments. I remember the demonstrations in some towns, such as Urosevac and elsewhere. The most important political protest was the strike of the miners in Trepca because they demanded that all Albanian officials in the Assembly of the Federation resign. Namely, all those who supported the constitutional amendments. One of them was Rrahman Morina, the president of the League of Communists of Kosovo. Another one, Ali Shukrija was a member of the presidency of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Then there was Hysamedin Azemi who was also a high official in the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the reaction to those demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The entire Yugoslav public was worried because of the strike of the miners, and the miners received telegrams stating support to their cause and the political consequences were very far reaching. Federal authorities had to act to protect the constitutional order and carry out its tasks and achieve the set goals. I remember that the Presidency of Yugoslavia introduced so-called special measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who had organised these demonstrations, and what triggered them?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were triggered mostly by false information, namely that the use of languages and scripts would be jeopardised by the amendments. Even strange things that the wearing of the Albanian folk hat would be prohibited, that normal life would no longer be the same, that equality was at stake, that the language would no longer be used officially. And the aim was to incite the people to resist constitutional changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see D008-6787.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's tab 5 in your binder. Tell us briefly what these conclusions of the Assembly of the SFRY mean. They were published on the 3rd of March, 1989.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as it says, for the purpose of protecting constitutional order, public law and order, the personal safety and security of all citizens, and also for the normalisation of the situation, the Assembly of the SFRY supports the decisions of the Presidency as the collective presidential body, and in these items the duties of the executive committee are defined at their levels of the republics and the provinces. The citizens are called upon to return to their regular work duties and activities. That criminal and other proceedings be launched against the organisers, of counter-revolutionary activity be launched. The Assembly does not support the demands of the minors because they believe that only the legal authorities can appoint officials or, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00905.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jokanovic, did the authorities of the Republic of Serbia, or could they do anything about these events and developments in February and March 1998?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The authorities of Serbia couldn't. The only thing that was in existence at the time were the so-called joint forces. They were forces from all republics and provinces, and the authorities from the Republic of Serbia were only able to do something to raise certain issues through federal institutions but not directly in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your position in March 1989?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said at the outset when I introduced myself, on that date the 23rd of March, 1989, I was president of the Assembly of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did the Assembly of Kosovo meet, at which meeting did it support the amendments of the constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March of that year. The Assembly of Vojvodina had held its meeting on the 10th of March. They had already approved the amendments to the constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And which year was this, the 23rd of March of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many delegates took part in the work of the Assembly of Kosovo on the 23rd of March, 1989?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly of Kosovo had a total of 190 delegates. The majority of delegates from all three chambers were present. Some were absent, that is three were absent, so that a total of 187 participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of the Assembly of Kosovo in March 1989?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic makeup was in keeping with the ethnic makeup of the population, I said as much in a previous answer. About 70 per cent were Albanians and the 30 per cent were persons of other ethnic affiliations, Serbs, Montenegrin, Turks, but 70 per cent were Albanians because that was one of the principles upheld in Kosovo in the system that was in existence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see D006-4413, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's tab 6. The document we are about to see is a recording of the joint session of all three chambers of the Assembly of Kosovo held on the 23rd of March, 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we now please see page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were there any guests at this session held on the 23rd of March, and if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This tape recording was translated into writing, but as you can see, I addressed those in attendance. Sinan Hasani was there, member of the SFRY Presidency, which is the body I described before; then comrade Sefcet Jasari, who was member of the presidency of Serbia; next Velimir Vukmanovic and Ferat Ahmeti, who were vice-presidents of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, one was Serbian and the other Albanian; next, it was the deputy of the constitutional commission of Serbia, I don't know who it was, as well as representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the media coverage this Assembly enjoyed?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was surprised as the speaker of the president of the Assembly by the exceptionally great interest for this session. There were 180 accredited journalists. Although I have had a rich political career, but on this occasion I was supposed to face the greatest number of journalists ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who gave the initial remarks?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I did, and you can see it in this tape recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which is your page 6 as well. This part has to do with your introductory remarks. You can see here, but perhaps you can tell us as well, what were the main points of your introductory remarks?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean what I can see on page 6 or what I can recall off the cuff?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell us what you can recall.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to briefly explain the gist of the problem and to point out that these amendments were not aimed as changing the constitutional status of the province of Kosovo within the federal state of Yugoslavia. As well as that these amendments had no intention of changing the status of the province in the Federation. Serbia was only to receive certain competencies which were standard competencies or powers of a state, and that the quality of languages and scripts in the province was to be guaranteed and regulated by the provincial constitution and body of law. The last thing I focused on, because it is important, was Amendment 47. It changed any veto powers of the provincial Assembly in favour of a more complex procedure which I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that. After your remarks, was there any discussion from the floor concerning this item on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The session developed in keeping with the agenda. There were contributions. Each delegate who request the floor had a chance to address the others. I think there were around 30 delegates contributing. They were all able to take the floor, and once the discussion was finished, we voted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By way of illustration, perhaps we can go to page 23 in the English and page 14 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You don't have to look for it in your hard copy, you have it on the screen. Those people who wanted to contribute, were they free to do so, and did they express their position concerning any item of the agenda?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: All those who contributed were free to do so. No one was interrupted, as you can see from the transcript. All those who voted against wanted to take the floor. Those in favour did not request it. That was rather indicative. Using the existing political system, the representatives used the opportunity to address the Assembly not only on their own behalf, but on behalf of their constituencies, these being socio-political organisations, municipalities, trade unions, associations of war veterans, youth associations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 25 in the B/C/S and 15 in the English version. Page 16, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, we see here Imer Dzafici taking the floor. Who did he represent, and whose position did he express? You can see it on the screen, Mr. Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I found it in my hard copy. The screen, yes. He was from the working bodies and organs of the Prizren Municipal Assembly, and he stated that there was intensive political discussion about the amendments, and he supported their position and stated to the Assembly that the Prizren municipal organ supported the changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I please ask that it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00906. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D011-4958.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 8. Mr. Jokanovic, your tab 8.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 8. Thank you. Do you want me to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the newspaper "Politika" which was the newspaper with the widest circulation in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please look at the screen. This is not "Politika".

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that's number 9. This is the "Rilindja" newspaper. I think they had the widest circulation in Kosovo in Albanian. And the title in Albanian it says "Agreement to the Amendments of the Serbian Constitution."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What does the journalist say? How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: According to this information, it says 180.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page, could we please see that. Who were the reporters?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Z. Celaj, Y. Baja, R. Rugova, R. Bislimi, and M. Gjata. Photo reporters, Skenderi and Bylykbashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I seek to -- could we please MFI this document pending its translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document which is D011-4658 shall be exhibited as D00907 marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have D011-4962.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the "Politika". It is similar to the "Rilindja" except that it was published in Belgrade. They were reporting on the work of the Assembly stating that the amendments were approved by the Municipal Assembly. They also referred to those in attendance and have parts of the stenogram on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The introductory part, can we see here the results of the Assembly vote?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It says 24 people took the floor. I thought there were around 30. The amendments were adopted by a vast majority. Out of 180, 10 were against and 2 abstained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I seek to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, it should be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, it will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00908 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we next have D011-5052, which is a video recording.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The booths did not receive any transcript of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, this excerpt, can you tell us what we just saw?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw myself, but I was much younger then. I stated that the amendments were adopted, well, I looked sort of nice. I realise now that it was more of a ceremony. The delegates after I declared the adoption gave a standing ovation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After it this portion of the session, did the Assembly resume its work?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After a 20-minute break, we resumed work, but not in joint session. I no longer presided it, the people broke up into chambers. First of all, there were introductory remarks by the vice-president of the government or by the deputy prime minister, Mr. Fusuri [phoen]. Other agenda items were discussed as well, and judges were appointed as well as court presidents and prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, could we have P8.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, I seek to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How is that going to help us, Mr. Djurdjic? It's a short video. It shows a public gathering. We've been told by the witness the effect of it and what it is. The extent of this detail troubles us, but we are not stopping you, but this video is just too far. The amendments were carried. That's the significant issue that I think you want to put forward, and they were carried with wide support.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wanted to do all this because I would later present certain statements to the witness so as to comment on the contents. I simply wanted to provide a basis before that. I don't want to explain it too widely in front of the witness. And we are approaching that crucial moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We won't receive the video, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokanovic, we have this exhibit, it's already part of the case file. This was the decision to pass Amendments 9 to 49 to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. Could we only go through those amendments which I believe are the most important. We have touched upon it in the course of your testimony. Could we go to page 23 of the English. It is your Amendment 27. It is your page 317 in the upper right-hand side corner.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: 27, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: A brief comment, please.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This amendment speaks of the equality of the languages and scripts across the territory of Serbia. I believe it is important for your case and in particular the last paragraph where we have a guarantee of that equality. It says that under this constitution provincial constitution shall identify which languages of the ethnic community shall be equal and that the province shall ensure that equality of the languages spoken and the alphabets as guaranteed by the republican constitution, the provincial institution also provided guarantees of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 31 in the English version, and it's page 320 in the lower right corner. It's Amendment 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I am interested in items 3 and 4. Could you briefly comment.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Item 3, that's the essential thing about which I have already spoken. Namely the issue of people's defence and the basis for the plans and preparations for the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about item 4?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Item 4, the Territorial Defence, namely the managing of the Territorial Defence as a matter of interest for the entire republic, but a Territorial Defence exists also in the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please turn the page and comment on the last paragraph. That's on page 35 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Which amendment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 33, the last paragraph of that amendment. And it ends on page 321. Before Amendment 34, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Amendment 34 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph before that amendment.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: "This amendment shall supersede the relevant parts and supplement the provisions of Article 300 and shall supersede Article 423 of the constitution of Serbia." This elaborates some matters which were not precisely defined and some basic state functions are regulated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 48 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And in your binder, it's page 326. That's Amendment 45.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Court of Kosovo was in existence, and it still has all its powers even after these amendments, but it is stated here that the Supreme Court decides about legal issues, about things that are regulated and the Criminal Code of the republic. And it also decides in a third instance about the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 49 of the English version, and for you it's Amendment 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, our translation is referring to the Supreme Court of Serbia. The witness was speaking of the Supreme Court of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, please tell us, what does the Supreme Court of Serbia decide about under these amendments?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is about the Supreme Court of Serbia. This amendment defines the powers of the Supreme Court of Serbia to decide about extraordinary legal remedies under the Criminal Code of Serbia, because before these amendments, the Supreme Court of the province was the highest legal instance. But I mentioned extraordinary legal remedies, that and the death penalty are now matters decided upon by the Supreme Court of Serbia in the third instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 49 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And its page 47 in your binder, the last amendment. Please explain the essence of this amendment.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Amendment 47 changes the right of veto and the principle of approval. It changes a complex procedure. If the Assemblies of the provinces fail to approve, then a special group is established and within six months --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am afraid the interpreters missed part of that answer. And it will need to be repeated, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said here, or rather, it was recorded that after six months -- don't you look at this but listen to me instead. So the last thing that was recorded was within six months of what, please repeat your entire answer about the essence of this amendment, but please slowly.

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The essence of this amendment is to allow for the possibility that the Republic of Serbia changes its constitution without being prevented by veto. Instead of a veto, this amendment lays out a complex procedure of finding agreement with a provincial Assemblies to find a solution. And if that solution is not found, the proposal cannot go before the Assembly of Serbia. The eventual, or rather, the last resort is a referendum by which the decision on changing the constitution of Serbia is carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this Assembly session was held, was the Assembly of SAP Kosovo visited by a delegation?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after this Assembly meeting, or rather, a few days later, I don't recall exactly how much, we received a visit from the parliamentary delegation of the council of Europe. We discussed the situation in Kosovo and the constitutional changes. I informed the delegation about the situation in Kosovo and about the session of the provincial Assembly as well as of the adoption of these amendments. I explained to them the essence of these changes. The talks were constructive, and they were friendly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were there any objections to the work of the Assembly of Kosovo which carried the amendments to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The parliamentary delegation raised no objections to me. After the talk we had, they wanted to meet Mr. Rugova and Mr. Djosaj [phoen] and another gentleman whose name escapes me now. I agreed and I promised them that we would invite these persons to the Assembly, but a member of that delegation called somebody up on the phone and said he would call back. On the following day, I was informed that the talk with Rugova and some other persons who were politically active at the time had taken place in hotel rooms at the Grand Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did they speak to the delegates who voted against the amendments?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: When the parliamentary delegation left for Belgrade and met the president of the federal Executive Council Mr. Ante Markovic and other high officials, I learned that this delegation wanted to speak to those members of the Assembly subsequently. I said, Why not, we can make that possible, but Ante Markovic replied, You are not in charge of foreign policy, I am. And he sent a plane to Pristina so that these people travelled to Belgrade and spoke to the parliamentary delegation of the council of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: There's one more thing I would like to know, did the Assembly of Kosovo also carry the amendments to the constitution of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In June or July, with regard to these amendments to the constitution of Serbia, the, or rather, following up on these amendments, the Assembly of Kosovo adopted its own amendments, they were carried and harmonised to the amendments of the constitution of Serbia, and some other amendments to the constitution of Yugoslavia which have to do with the further development of self-management and social relations. These amendments were carried by the Assembly of Kosovo unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were there political tensions when these amendments to the constitution of Kosovo were carried?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The Assembly session went normally and these amendments were carried unanimously by the Kosovo Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see our transcript, namely page 248. That's the 28th of January, 2009. Page 248, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'll read to you, Mr. Jokanovic, part of the statement of witness Surroi. To the question in March 1989 too was there a vote about these amendments in the Assembly of Kosovo. The witness replied: "Well, that's what they called it. They were carried, but it wasn't that way because all around the building of the parliament there were armoured vehicles. The entire Kosovo population was under pressure and especially the members of the Assembly, and there were people in the building who voted without even being members of the Assembly of Kosovo?" Let me ask you, were there armoured vehicles around the building of the Assembly of Kosovo on the 23rd of March, 1989?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no armoured vehicles around the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the members of the Assembly pressurized with regard to their participation, debate, or their vote?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, the members of the Assembly consulted their constituencies and voted the way they thought fit. Some were in favour, some were against.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did persons vote without being members of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't possible. Whoever wasn't a member of the Assembly couldn't vote. There were guests, but they didn't vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As there were many journalists present, we have seen them, have you seen any photograph of an armoured vehicle around the Assembly building on the day of the vote?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: If there had been armoured vehicles and the rest as stated by this witness, then probably some of the numerous journalists would have recorded that. That would have been very interesting to the domestic public and especially to the international public because there were both Yugoslav journalists from all over Yugoslavia and also foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see the transcript of the 13th of March, 2009. Page 2201.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll see part of the statement of witness Adnan Merovci who on this page line 4 says, the constitutional amendments which were imposed by force against the will of the people and although the part of the public was against him, the regime implemented a measure to -- this measure to the effect of destroying all the institutions from the lowest to the highest levels including education system, health system, police system, et cetera. Could you comment?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think this statement is untrue because these amendments only pertain to what I've already had the opportunity to speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see our transcript of the 18th of June, 2009. Page 6250.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's part of the statement of the witness Baton Haxhiu who in lines 1 through 3 says: "The entire problem started with the constitutional changes in 1989. The main problem of Kosovo is dated the 23rd of March, 1989 when the constitution was changed." Mr. Jokanovic, after the adoption of the constitution, were there any changes to the autonomy of Kosovo? Were any institutions of Autonomous Province of Kosovo abolished or suspended?

utterances.speaker: VUKASIN JOKANOVIC
utterances.text: After these amendments there were amendments to the constitution of Kosovo. Following that, Reza Suponji [phoen] was elected a member of the Presidency of the Yugoslavia. After these amendments, the constitution of Kosovo was changed and the Assembly -- and I was re-elected for another one year as president of the Assembly. I expressed my gratitude to the Assembly for the co-operation and for the results we achieved. And toward the end of the year, in December, 1989, new elections were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see Exhibit P286.
